texts.0: SP, due to a late decision on when the unusual attitude had been resolved, did not transition from recovery inputs to level-flight control and left the pitch attitude uncaptured at the horizon. The altitude ran beyond 300 feet from the recovery reference and continued to diverge. IP had to intervene on the controls to establish level flight, and SP did not recognize the excursion before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed pitch capture at the horizon after the roll to wings level, allowed the altitude to run out to the 300 foot limit before any correction was made. The correction was initiated only after verbal prompting from the IP and the return to the reference altitude was slow. Altitude control after the recovery stayed at the outer edge of the standard for the remainder of the exercise.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete pitch capture at the horizon, allowed the altitude to deviate between 150 and 300 feet from the recovery reference once the aircraft was back in controlled flight. SP recognized the trend without prompting and returned to level flight with a smooth pitch and power adjustment. No IP intervention was required and the following recoveries were flown tighter.
texts.3: SP established level flight immediately on completion of each recovery and held the altitude within 150 feet of the recovery reference. The pitch capture at the horizon was positive, without overshoot, and altitude was stabilized before the next input was called for.
texts.4: SP captured level flight exactly at the horizon with negligible altitude excursion from the recovery reference. Pitch control through the transition from recovery to level flight was continuous, and the altitude was frozen at the first attempt on every attitude presented.
texts.marginal: SP kept the post-recovery altitude inside standards but arrested the excursion close to 150 feet on most attitudes rather than well within it. The trend was a pitch capture applied slightly late rather than anticipated at the horizon. SP is expected to lead the level-off and stabilize the altitude earlier in subsequent recoveries.

texts_at.1: SP established level flight immediately on completion of each recovery, holding the altitude within approximately 280 feet of the recovery reference, at the outer edge of the standard, due to a pitch capture at the horizon that settled a moment after wings level rather than together with it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to capture the pitch at the same instant the wings come level.
texts_at.2: SP established level flight on completion of each recovery, holding the altitude within about 220 feet of the recovery reference, due to a power adjustment applied a beat after the pitch capture rather than with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring power and pitch together at the level-off.
texts_at.3: SP established level flight on completion of each recovery within approximately 110 feet of the recovery reference, due to a pitch capture at the horizon that was positive but held a fraction past the exact level-flight attitude before settling. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to stop the pitch capture precisely at the horizon rather than easing past it.

texts_above.2: SP captured level flight positively at the horizon on completion of every recovery, holding the altitude within about 180 feet of the recovery reference with no overshoot requiring correction. Freezing the pitch a fraction sooner at the horizon would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude capture.
texts_above.3: SP captured level flight at the horizon with negligible overshoot on every recovery, holding the altitude within roughly 60 feet of the recovery reference from the first attempt. The only refinement available was to fold the power adjustment into the same instant as the pitch capture. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude control.
texts_above.4: SP captured level flight exactly at the horizon with negligible altitude excursion from the recovery reference on every attitude, with pitch control through the transition from recovery to level flight continuous and the altitude frozen at the first attempt. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent altitude capture.

texts.0: SP, due to power that was not matched to the attitude during the recovery, left the throttle in the entry setting through the pitch change and did not re-establish the level-flight airspeed. From the nose-low attitudes the airspeed built more than 20 knots above the reference and from the nose-high attitudes it decayed more than 20 knots below it. IP had to take the throttle to bring the aircraft back inside the airspeed limits.
texts.1: SP, due to a power adjustment applied after the pitch input rather than with it, allowed the airspeed to reach the 20 knot limit from the reference before the throttle was moved. The correction was made only after the IP called the airspeed, and the return to the reference speed lagged the return to level flight. Airspeed control remained at the outer edge of the standard on each recovery.
texts.2: SP, due to a small mismatch between throttle movement and rate of pitch change, allowed the airspeed to deviate between 10 and 20 knots from the level-flight reference after the recovery. SP detected the trend on the airspeed indicator without prompting and restored the reference speed with a single, correctly sized power adjustment. No IP action on the throttle was required.
texts.3: SP matched the power to the changing attitude throughout each recovery and held the post-recovery airspeed within 10 knots of the level-flight reference. The throttle was moved with the pitch input rather than after it, so no airspeed chase developed.
texts.4: SP anticipated the airspeed effect of each attitude and set the power accordingly, holding the post-recovery airspeed essentially on the level-flight reference. There was no overshoot in either direction and no secondary throttle correction was needed on any of the attitudes flown.
texts.marginal: SP held the post-recovery airspeed inside standards but repeatedly let it approach 10 knots from the reference before the power correction was applied. The pattern was a throttle input that followed the pitch input instead of accompanying it. SP is expected to lead the power with the attitude change so the airspeed stays closer to the reference in later sorties.

texts_at.1: SP matched power to the changing attitude through each recovery and held the post-recovery airspeed within approximately 18 knots of the level-flight reference, at the outer edge of the standard, due to a throttle movement started a beat after the pitch input rather than with it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to move the throttle in the same instant as the pitch input.
texts_at.2: SP held the post-recovery airspeed within about 15 knots of the level-flight reference on each recovery, due to a power adjustment sized correctly but applied a moment after the attitude had already changed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to lead the power change with the attitude rather than follow it.
texts_at.3: SP held the post-recovery airspeed within approximately 8 knots of the level-flight reference on each recovery, due to a throttle movement that trailed the pitch input by a fraction rather than matching it exactly. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to move power and pitch together so no small chase remains.

texts_above.2: SP moved the throttle with the pitch input on every recovery, holding the post-recovery airspeed within about 15 knots of the level-flight reference with no chase developing. Leading the power change by a fraction earlier on the fastest recoveries would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound power management.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated the airspeed effect of each attitude on every recovery and set the power accordingly, holding the airspeed within a few knots of the level-flight reference with no overshoot in either direction. The technique is already sound; nothing in the throttle timing needs to change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to disciplined power-to-pitch coordination.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the airspeed effect of each attitude and set the power accordingly on every recovery, holding the post-recovery airspeed essentially on the level-flight reference with no overshoot and no secondary throttle correction needed on any of the attitudes flown. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional power management.

texts.0: SP, due to a roll-out that was not referenced to any heading, stopped the recovery wherever the wings happened to level and made no attempt to fly a defined exit heading. The exit heading was more than 10 degrees from the intended heading and the aircraft continued to drift in heading afterwards. IP had to direct the aircraft back onto the working heading for the next presentation.
texts.1: SP, due to a roll rate that was not reduced approaching wings level, overshot the intended exit heading and stopped at the 10 degree limit. The heading was regained only after the IP called it, and the correction was made with a shallow turn that took an extended period. Exit heading accuracy stayed at the outer edge of the standard on the following attitudes.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late reduction of roll rate at wings level, exited the recovery between 5 and 10 degrees from the intended heading. SP identified the offset on the heading indicator without prompting and corrected back with a small, coordinated turn before the next attitude was set. No IP prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP rolled out on the intended exit heading within 5 degrees on each recovery. The roll rate was reduced approaching wings level so that heading was captured on the first attempt without a subsequent correcting turn.
texts.4: SP exited every recovery on the intended heading with negligible offset, capturing it directly out of the roll with no overshoot. Heading, wings level and level pitch were achieved in the same moment rather than in sequence.
texts.marginal: SP exited the recoveries inside the heading standard but with an offset that sat near 5 degrees more often than not, always in the direction of the roll. The trend was a roll rate carried slightly too long into wings level. SP is expected to anticipate the roll-out and stop the heading precisely on the intended value.

texts_at.1: SP rolled out approximately 9 degrees from the intended exit heading on each recovery, at the outer edge of the standard, due to a roll rate reduced only as wings level was reached rather than during the last part of the roll. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to begin reducing the roll rate before wings level rather than at the moment it is reached.
texts_at.2: SP exited each recovery approximately 7 degrees from the intended heading, due to a roll rate that eased a beat after wings level rather than in anticipation of it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to anticipate wings level and reduce the roll rate before it arrives.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out within approximately 4 degrees of the intended exit heading on each recovery, due to a roll rate reduced a fraction after the heading indicator confirmed the approach to wings level rather than in anticipation of it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate the heading indicator rather than confirm it after the fact.

texts_above.2: SP reduced the roll rate approaching wings level on every recovery and rolled out within about 7 degrees of the intended exit heading, with no subsequent correcting turn required. Anticipating the reduction a fraction earlier would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid heading capture.
texts_above.3: SP captured heading, wings level and level pitch essentially together on every recovery, rolling out within a degree or two of the intended exit heading with no correction to follow. The only refinement available was to anticipate the roll-rate reduction a fraction earlier still. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed heading control.
texts_above.4: SP exited every recovery on the intended heading with negligible offset, capturing it directly out of the roll with no overshoot, with heading, wings level and level pitch achieved in the same moment rather than in sequence. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding heading capture.

texts.0: SP, due to a failure to read the bank angle and its direction before acting, rolled the aircraft away from the nearest horizon and took the long way round to wings level. The extended roll left the exit heading more than 10 degrees from the intended value and added altitude loss beyond 300 feet. IP had to take control and roll the aircraft level in the correct direction.
texts.1: SP, due to an attitude assessment made from the nose position alone without reading bank, started the roll in the wrong direction and reversed it only after the IP called the correct direction. The reversal left the exit heading at the 10 degree limit and delayed the level-off. The correct roll direction was applied on later attitudes only after the same verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief hesitation in identifying which horizon was nearer, started the roll late and initially at too low a rate. SP corrected the roll direction and rate without prompting and reached wings level with an exit heading between 5 and 10 degrees from the intended value. The level-off was completed without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP read the bank angle correctly on every attitude and rolled towards the nearest horizon without hesitation. The roll was made at a rate appropriate to the bank presented and wings level was reached on the shortest available path.
texts.4: SP identified the nearest horizon instantly on every presentation, including the high-bank attitudes, and rolled directly to wings level by the shortest path. The direction decision was never revised and the roll rate was matched to the bank throughout.
texts.marginal: SP consistently rolled towards the nearest horizon but with a short pause between recognizing the attitude and committing to the roll. The direction chosen was always correct and the exit parameters stayed inside standards. SP is expected to shorten the recognition-to-input interval so the roll begins as the attitude is read.

texts_at.1: SP read the bank angle correctly and rolled toward the nearest horizon on every attitude, due to a brief check of the nose position before the bank was confirmed rather than the two being read together. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read bank and nose position in the same glance.
texts_at.2: SP rolled toward the nearest horizon on every attitude, due to a rate of roll set a moment after the direction was confirmed rather than together with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the roll rate in the same instant the direction is confirmed.
texts_at.3: SP read the bank angle correctly on every attitude and rolled toward the nearest horizon without hesitation, due to a roll rate that settled toward the shortest-path value a fraction after the input began rather than from the first movement. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the final roll rate with the very first input.

texts_above.2: SP read the bank angle correctly on every attitude and rolled toward the nearest horizon at a rate matched to the bank presented, reaching wings level on the shortest available path each time. Committing to that rate with the very first input would sharpen the roll further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady horizon-recovery judgement.
texts_above.3: SP matched the roll rate to the bank presented on every attitude and reached wings level on the shortest path with no direction ever revised. The only refinement available was to commit to the final roll rate from the first movement of the stick. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate horizon-recovery judgement.
texts_above.4: SP identified the nearest horizon instantly on every presentation, including the high-bank attitudes, and rolled directly to wings level by the shortest path, with the direction decision never revised and the roll rate matched to the bank throughout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary horizon-recovery judgement.

texts.0: SP, due to stress in the evaluated environment that produced a pull towards the horizon instead of an unload, increased angle of attack in a decaying nose-high attitude and allowed the stall to develop. Airspeed fell more than 20 knots below the level-flight reference with the stick shaker active and the aircraft departed the intended flight path. IP took control to unload the wing and complete the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to stress that delayed the sequence of power, roll and unload in the nose-high attitude, held back pressure while the airspeed decayed to the 20 knot limit and buffet onset was reached. The wing was unloaded only after the IP called the airspeed and the buffet. The margin to the stall was restored, but only through verbal intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly delayed unload after the roll in the nose-high attitude, allowed the airspeed to decay between 10 and 20 knots below the level-flight reference before angle of attack was reduced. SP recognized the decay on the airspeed indicator, unloaded and added power without prompting, and no buffet developed. The remaining nose-high attitudes were flown with the unload applied on time.
texts.3: SP applied power, rolled towards the nearest horizon and unloaded the wing in the correct order on every nose-high attitude, so that no approach to the stall developed. Airspeed was never allowed to decay more than 10 knots below the level-flight reference during the recovery.
texts.4: SP flew every nose-high recovery with the angle of attack reduced before the airspeed could decay, keeping a clear margin to the stall at all times. Power, roll and unload were applied as one coordinated action and there was no indication of approach to the stall at any point.
texts.marginal: SP avoided any approach to the stall in the nose-high attitudes but let the airspeed run down closer to the 10 knot band than required before unloading. The unload was correct in technique yet applied late in the sequence. SP is expected to unload the wing as the roll is started rather than after wings level is reached.

texts_at.1: SP applied power, rolled toward the nearest horizon and unloaded the wing on every nose-high attitude, allowing the airspeed to decay to approximately 18 knots below the level-flight reference before angle of attack was reduced, at the outer edge of the standard, due to stress at the attitude that shortened the interval spent reading the airspeed trend. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the airspeed indicator into the scan earlier in the roll so the unload is not delayed by the stress response.
texts_at.2: SP unloaded the wing on every nose-high attitude with the airspeed decaying to about 15 knots below the level-flight reference before the reduction, due to a residual stress response that shortened the time spent cross-checking airspeed during the roll. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to manage the stress response before the roll starts so the airspeed cross-check is not compressed.
texts_at.3: SP applied power, rolled and unloaded the wing in the correct order on every nose-high attitude, keeping the airspeed decay to approximately 8 knots below the level-flight reference, due to a stress response at the attitude that was managed but still shortened the margin taken before unloading. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to build a wider margin into the unload despite the stress response.

texts_above.2: SP applied power, rolled towards the nearest horizon and unloaded the wing in the correct order on every nose-high attitude, holding the airspeed decay to about 15 knots below the level-flight reference with no buffet developing. Starting the unload a fraction earlier in the roll would widen that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable stall-margin management.
texts_above.3: SP flew every nose-high recovery with the angle of attack reduced well before the airspeed could decay significantly, keeping a clear and repeatable margin to the stall despite the demands of the attitude. The only refinement available was to start the unload a fraction earlier still in the roll. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good stall-margin management.
texts_above.4: SP flew every nose-high recovery with the angle of attack reduced before the airspeed could decay, keeping a clear margin to the stall at all times, with power, roll and unload applied as one coordinated action and no indication of approach to the stall at any point. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior stall-margin management.

error_modes.label: SPLIT-S AVOIDANCE IN NOSE-LOW AND INVERTED RECOVERY

texts.0: SP, due to a pull applied before the bank was removed, initiated back pressure while the aircraft was still inverted and effectively started a Split-S from the recovery attitude. Altitude loss exceeded 300 feet and continued to increase while the nose remained below the horizon. IP took control to roll the aircraft upright and arrest the descent.
texts.1: SP, due to an incorrect order of inputs from the inverted attitude, began the pull before wings level was reached and reversed the sequence only after the IP called for the roll first. Altitude loss reached the 300 foot limit before the nose was raised. The correct roll-then-pull sequence was applied on later attitudes only after the same prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a slight overlap between the roll and the pull from the nose-low inverted attitude, started raising the nose before the bank was fully removed. SP recognized the overlap without prompting, completed the roll first and then raised the nose, keeping the altitude loss between 150 and 300 feet. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP removed the bank before applying any back pressure on every nose-low and inverted attitude, so no Split-S tendency developed. The roll-then-pull sequence was applied cleanly and the nose was raised only once the wings were level.
texts.4: SP separated the roll and the pull precisely on every inverted and nose-low attitude, with back pressure introduced only after wings level. There was never any tendency towards a Split-S and the recovery path was the shortest available in each case.
texts.marginal: SP kept the correct roll-then-pull sequence on all nose-low and inverted attitudes, but the pull was started just as the wings arrived at level rather than clearly after. The technique stayed within standards and no Split-S tendency appeared. SP is expected to keep a firmer separation between removing bank and raising the nose.

texts_at.1: SP removed the bank before applying back pressure on every nose-low and inverted attitude, holding the altitude loss to approximately 280 feet, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the pull beginning a beat before the wings were fully confirmed level rather than clearly after. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm wings level before beginning any back pressure.
texts_at.2: SP removed the bank before applying back pressure on every attitude, holding the altitude loss to about 220 feet, due to a small overlap between the last part of the roll and the first part of the pull rather than the two being fully separated. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the roll fully before starting the pull.
texts_at.3: SP removed the bank before applying any back pressure on every nose-low and inverted attitude, holding the altitude loss to approximately 110 feet, due to the pull beginning a fraction sooner than the technique calls for once the wings appeared level. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold a firmer separation between removing bank and raising the nose.

texts_above.2: SP removed the bank before applying any back pressure on every nose-low and inverted attitude, holding the altitude loss to about 180 feet with no Split-S tendency developing. Holding the separation a fraction longer on the fastest reversals would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured sequencing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP separated the roll and the pull cleanly on every inverted and nose-low attitude, holding the altitude loss to roughly 60 feet with back pressure introduced only once the wings were unmistakably level. The only refinement available was to hold that separation a fraction longer still on the steepest attitudes. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise sequencing discipline.
texts_above.4: SP separated the roll and the pull precisely on every inverted and nose-low attitude, with back pressure introduced only after wings level, no tendency towards a Split-S at any point and the recovery path the shortest available in each case. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate sequencing discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to overconfidence in the margin available at the entry airspeed, applied an abrupt and large pull out of the nose-low attitude without regard for the load and speed limits. The recovery was flown with the airspeed running beyond the 20 knot band and the pull carried towards the aircraft limits. IP intervened on the controls to reduce the load and contain the airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to an overconfident assessment of how quickly the nose could be raised, applied back pressure at a rate that brought the aircraft up against its limits and required an IP call to ease the pull. Airspeed reached the 20 knot limit during the recovery before the load was reduced. Limits were respected only after the verbal correction.
texts.2: SP, due to a pull rate slightly larger than the situation required, moved the recovery closer to the load and airspeed margins than necessary. SP recognized the trend on the instruments, eased the back pressure and completed the recovery with the airspeed between 10 and 20 knots of the reference. The limits were not approached again on the following attitudes.
texts.3: SP completed every recovery within the aircraft load and airspeed limits, using a pull rate matched to the attitude and the energy state. No limit was approached and the recovery was still completed promptly.
texts.4: SP flew every recovery with a comfortable margin to the load and airspeed limits while still resolving the attitude at the first opportunity. The control inputs were sized precisely to the attitude presented, with no unnecessary loading of the aircraft.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the aircraft limits on every recovery but used a pull rate on the nose-low attitudes that left less margin than necessary. No limit was exceeded and the parameters remained inside standards. SP is expected to size the pull to the actual attitude and energy state rather than applying a uniformly aggressive input.

texts_at.1: SP completed every recovery within the aircraft load and airspeed limits, with airspeed reaching approximately 18 knots of the reference during the pull, at the outer edge of the standard, due to a rate of back pressure sized on the assumption that the margin was larger than it actually was. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to judge the pull rate from the actual margin available rather than an assumed one.
texts_at.2: SP completed every recovery within the aircraft limits, with airspeed reaching about 15 knots of the reference, due to a pull rate sized slightly larger than the attitude required. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to match the pull rate more closely to the attitude and energy state presented.
texts_at.3: SP completed every recovery within the aircraft load and airspeed limits, with airspeed held to approximately 8 knots of the reference, due to a pull rate that still carried a degree of built-in caution rather than being sized exactly to the attitude. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the pull to the attitude itself rather than to a cautious margin.

texts_above.2: SP completed every recovery within the aircraft load and airspeed limits, using a pull rate matched to the attitude and holding airspeed within about 15 knots of the reference with the recovery still completed promptly. Sizing the pull a fraction more finely to the energy state would widen the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent limit management.
texts_above.3: SP flew every recovery with a comfortable and consistent margin to the load and airspeed limits while still resolving the attitude at the first opportunity, with the control inputs sized precisely to the attitude presented. The technique is already sound; nothing in the pull-rate judgement needs to change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to disciplined limit management.
texts_above.4: SP flew every recovery with a comfortable margin to the load and airspeed limits while still resolving the attitude at the first opportunity, with control inputs sized precisely to the attitude presented and no unnecessary loading of the aircraft at any point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless limit management.

error_modes.label: MINIMUM ALTITUDE LOSS AND PROMPTNESS OF RECOVERY

texts.0: SP, due to a long pause between the transfer of control and the first recovery input, allowed the nose-low attitudes to develop further before acting. Altitude loss exceeded 300 feet on the recoveries and the descent was still increasing when the IP took control to complete them. SP made no correction to the delay on subsequent presentations.
texts.1: SP, due to a hesitation in committing to the recovery inputs, started the roll and the pull late enough that altitude loss reached the 300 foot limit. The inputs were applied only after the IP prompted for the recovery to begin. The reaction time did not improve without repeated verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a short delay in reading the attitude before acting, started the recovery slightly late and lost between 150 and 300 feet in the process. SP recognized the delay and shortened the reaction time on the following attitudes without any prompting. IP intervention was not required at any point.
texts.3: SP began the recovery immediately on assuming control and completed it with the altitude loss held within 150 feet. Recognition, roll and pull followed each other without pause, so the attitude was resolved at the first opportunity.
texts.4: SP resolved every unusual attitude with negligible altitude loss, acting on the attitude the moment control was transferred. The recovery was complete before the aircraft state could develop further, on both the nose-high and the nose-low presentations.
texts.marginal: SP recovered from all attitudes with the altitude loss inside standards, but with a consistent short pause before the first input. The recoveries themselves were correct once started. texts_at.2: SP began the recovery promptly on every attitude, holding the altitude loss to about 220 feet, due to a short pause between assuming control and committing to the roll and pull. texts_above.3: SP began the recovery immediately on assuming control on every attitude, holding the altitude loss to roughly 60 feet with recognition, roll and pull following each other without pause. The only refinement available was to shorten the interval fractionally further on the highest-energy attitudes. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good recovery promptness.
texts_above.4: SP resolved every unusual attitude with negligible altitude loss, acting on the attitude the moment control was transferred, with the recovery complete before the aircraft state could develop further on both the nose-high and the nose-low presentations. texts.0: SP, due to spatial disorientation on assuming control with no immediate external horizon reference, misread the attitude and applied inputs appropriate to the opposite pitch and bank. The wrong inputs drove the altitude beyond 300 feet from the reference and the airspeed beyond the 20 knot band. IP took control and re-established the aircraft in level flight before returning it to SP.
texts.1: SP, due to an attitude read from a single instrument without cross-check, identified the pitch correctly but the bank incorrectly and began the recovery on that basis. The error was corrected only after the IP called the actual attitude, and by then the altitude had reached the 300 foot limit. SP continued to rely on a narrow scan for the remaining presentations.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that fixed briefly on the attitude indicator before including airspeed and altitude, was slow to build a complete picture of the aircraft state. SP completed the cross-check without prompting and recovered with the altitude between 150 and 300 feet of the reference. The scan was broadened on the following attitudes without IP input.
texts.3: SP read pitch, bank, airspeed and altitude in a single cross-check on assuming control and identified each attitude correctly before acting. The recovery inputs matched the actual aircraft state on every presentation and the parameters were held within the tighter tolerances.
texts.4: SP built a complete and correct picture of the aircraft state instantly on every presentation, including the high-bank and inverted attitudes. The cross-check was continuous through the recovery, so the inputs were adjusted as the state changed and the exit parameters were achieved with negligible deviation.

The picture was complete before the inputs were applied, only later than ideal. SP is expected to include energy state in the first sweep of the cross-check.

texts_at.1: SP read pitch, bank, airspeed and altitude in a cross-check on assuming control and identified each attitude correctly, holding the altitude within approximately 280 feet of the reference, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the cross-check settling on the attitude indicator a moment before airspeed and altitude were brought in. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring airspeed and altitude into the same first sweep as the attitude indicator.
texts_at.2: SP built a complete cross-check of pitch, bank, airspeed and altitude on every attitude, recovering with the altitude within about 220 feet of the reference, due to the airspeed and altitude being picked up a beat after the attitude indicator rather than in the same sweep. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to widen the first sweep of the cross-check to include energy state from the start.

error_modes.label: ZERO-G SYSTEM LIMITATIONS AND THE UNLOADED RECOVERY

texts.0: SP, due to unloading to near zero-G through the nose-high recovery without regard for the system limitations in that regime, held the unloaded condition through the roll and did not check for normal oil pressure indications once level flight was regained. The unloaded recovery cost more than 300 feet of altitude and the airspeed ran beyond the 20 knot band. IP took control, re-established positive G and completed the checks.
texts.1: SP, due to treating the unload as the whole of the recovery, maintained a near zero-G condition longer than the system limitations allow before rolling and raising the nose. Altitude loss reached the 300 foot limit and the oil pressure indications were checked only after the IP called for it. Positive G was restored on the same prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to holding the unload slightly longer than the attitude required, operated near zero-G for longer than intended during the nose-high recovery. SP restored positive G and checked the oil pressure indications without prompting, ending the recovery with the altitude between 150 and 300 feet of the reference. The following recoveries were flown with a shorter unload.
texts.3: SP unloaded only as far and as long as the nose-high attitude required, respecting the system limitations near zero-G, and checked for normal oil pressure indications on regaining level flight. Altitude loss was held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots of the reference.
texts.4: SP managed the unload precisely on every nose-high recovery, keeping the aircraft clear of prolonged near zero-G operation while still reducing angle of attack as required. Oil pressure indications were checked on each return to level flight and the deviations in altitude and airspeed were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept every recovery inside standards but held the unloaded condition close to zero-G slightly longer than the attitude called for, and the oil pressure check came late in the sequence. No system limitation was exceeded. SP is expected to limit the duration of the unload and to include the oil pressure check as part of the return to level flight.
